newsitem.title: USA: Mexico's Zedillo wants Clinton's respect:Newsweek.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Zedillo wants Clinton's respect:Newsweek.

text.p: The furore over the U.S. ratification of Mexico as a partner in the war on drugs may be revisited next week in Mexico City, where Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo will ask President Bill Clinton to show some respect, according to a published report.

"I will insist... that we are willing to do whatever is necessary (about drugs) as long as we have full respect for our own institutions and our sovereignty," Zedillo said in an interview with Newsweek Magazine published on Sunday.

"Drugs have become an issue because people feel that our sovereignty is threatened from abroad either by drug lords or by pressure from other countries to implement certain policies related to drug trafficking," Zedillo told Newsweek in a reference to U.S. pressure.
"Asked by the magazine if Mexico would become another Colombia, Zedillo replied:

"I hope we will be successful at stopping drug trafficking and persuading (traffickers) to go somewhere else. I'm not so optimistic about what will happen with drug trafficking as a global phenomenon."
Following its certification earlier this year, Mexican officials said that it was an insult to be part of the process and called for the United States to be certified as the world's top drug market.
In Washington, some members of Congress opposed Mexico's certification.

In February, a week before the certification decision, Mexico dismissed its top anti-narcotics official, Gen. Jesus Gutierrez, charging that he had ties to a drug kingpin. The general has been imprisoned on drug charges.

Newsweek magazine released Zedillo's interview on the day police announced that two federal judicial police agents investigating Mexico's most notorious drug lord were found dead in the trunk of a car in Mexico City.

Police found the bodies of agents Roberto Espinoza Mendoza and Marco Antonio Vazquez on Saturday inside a car parked outside a well-known restaurant, the Attorney General's office said in a statement.

Both agents were investigating Amado Carrillo Fuentes, the leader of the powerful Juarez cartel who is nicknamed "Lord of the Skies" for the huge quantities of cocaine he allegedly flies from Colombia, via Mexico, to the United States.
Mexico City daily Reforma said on Sunday that both bodies showed signs that they were executed.
In March, the United States and Mexico agreed on a common strategy to fight drug trafficking. The agreement pledged them to work together to combat drug use, production, trade and money laundering.
At the time, President Clinton's anti-drug czar, Gen. Barry McCaffrey told reporters that up to 70 percent of the illegal drugs entering the United States came via Mexico.
McCaffrey estimated that more than 300 tonnes of cocaine entered the U.S. each year.
A follow-up meeting of the U.S.-Mexican High Level Contact Group on Drug Control will take place in the United States in June of this year, the joint statement said.
